content: Aceclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) approved by the FDA for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, osteoarthritis, periarthritis of the scapulohumeral region, lumbago, ischialgia, and pain caused by non-articular rheumatism. Common adverse reactions include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, rash, redness, urticaria, enuresis symptoms, headache, dizziness, and drowsiness. The recommended adult dose is 200 mg daily, taken as a single dose every 24 hours. However, the dose and frequency may be adjusted under the supervision of a physician or pharmacist. There is limited information regarding off-label use in adults, both guideline-supported and non-guideline-supported. For pediatric patients, the dosage and indications are not established for children under six years of age. Similarly, there is limited information on off-label use in pediatric populations, whether guideline-supported or not. Aceclofenac is contraindicated in patients with allergies to the drug or its analogs (e.g., diclofenac), asthma, active peptic ulcers, or those who experience asthma, acute rhinitis, or urticaria triggered by NSAIDs, acetylsalicylic acid, or other prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors. Warnings include caution in patients with gastrointestinal disorders, a history of gastric ulceration, severe hepatic, cardiac, or renal impairment, those on diuretics, and those recovering from surgical treatment. Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials are generally reversible and minor, including gastrointestinal disorders (dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea), rash, redness, urticaria, enuresis symptoms, headache, dizziness, and drowsiness. Suspected adverse reactions can be reported to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088. Postmarketing experience data is limited. No specific drug interactions have been reported, but close monitoring is advised for patients taking aceclofenac in combination with lithium, digoxin, oral antidiabetic agents, anticoagulants, diuretics, or other analgesics. Aceclofenac should be avoided during pregnancy and lactation due to insufficient safety data. There is no FDA guidance on its use during labor and delivery, in geriatric populations, or in specific gender, racial, renal, hepatic, or immunocompromised patient groups. In cases of overdose, there is no human data available. Supportive and symptomatic treatment should be provided for complications such as hypotension, gastrointestinal irritation, respiratory depression, and convulsions. The mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of aceclofenac are not well-documented in the drug label. Clinical studies are also limited. Aceclofenac is supplied in blister packs containing 10 tablets each. It should be stored in tightly sealed containers at room temperature, not exceeding 30°C, and used within three years of the manufacturing date or before the printed expiration date. There is no established interaction between alcohol and aceclofenac, but patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while on this medication. Brand names for aceclofenac include Acent, Acenal, Acelofan, and Acelom. There is limited information on look-alike drug names for aceclofenac.
